# Who gets asked

## No one asks the **[Data Scientist]{.accent}**… {.center}

::: {.notes}
No one asks the person who actually has to write the code.

Legitimacy beat, gently: "I've been that programmer. I spent the last
few years moving a team from dplyr to Polars, and that migration is
where everything in this talk comes from."
:::

## Thesis: {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
*A language migration should optimize for the easiest option for the person who has to write the code.*
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM, SLOWLY)
The hot take: the API matters more than speed, cost, or support.

This is the one decision that determines how much friction the team absorbs.
:::

::: {.fragment}
We use a migration from my experience — **dplyr → Polars** — as the worked example to demostrate our thinking.
:::

::: {.fragment}
You can swap in your own, the concepts carry across any code migration.
:::

## By "API" I mean the function signature {auto-animate="true"}

Not a web API. The shape of the contract: what you pass in, what you
get back, what you have to learn to use it.

::: {.api-example}
**The `sum` API**

```r
sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Quick fence around the word before going on: API here is the literal
function signature — the arguments and the return — not REST.

"This is the sum API." Don't explain it. Next.
:::

## By "API" I mean the function signature {auto-animate="true"}

Not a web API. The shape of the contract: what you pass in, what you
get back, what you have to learn to use it.

::: {.api-example}
**The `filter` API**

```python
df.filter(pl.col("paid"))
```
:::

::: {.notes}
"This is the filter API." Same idea, different language. Move.
:::

# What "easiest" actually means

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM) My thesis called for optimizing for the "easiest" migration options. This is what I mean.
:::

## Easiest means: productive on day one {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- [Early]{.accent} wins

- The [thin-slice]{.accent} effect
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM):
Can the Data Scientist be productive immediately?

[click] 
Early wins — real code that runs on day one, before anyone has
mastered environments, classes, or types. 

Impresses superiors; feels good to accomplish things.

[click] 
Thin-slice theory, a well established psychological phenomenom:
First impressions aren't accurate, but they have more predictive power and persistence than we'd like. We're judgemental
animals. 

Callback: my first ten minutes installing Python was that thin slice. Everyone has had that, and it's not limited to programming, obviously.

Not fair, but real, and it has to be managed.
:::

## {.code-stack}

::: {.fragment}
**dplyr**

```r
library(dplyr)

df |>
  filter(status == "paid") |>
  select(
    is_customer = str_detect(persona, 'cust'), 
    revenue = sum(c_across(starts_with('res')))
  )
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Polars**

```python
from polars.selectors import *
from polars import col as c

df.filter(c.status == "paid").select(
    is_customer = c.persona.str.contains('cust'), 
    revenue = pl.sum_horizontal(starts_with('rev'))
    )
```
:::

::: {.fragment .center}
**Easiest = it works in ten minutes.**
:::

::: {.notes}
[click] 
dplyr for instance is a pipeline-based expressions friendly dataframe DSL.


[click] 
In polars, we get the main verbs 1:1.
The filter is basically identical.
We notice the selection is basically the same plus a new way of referencing.


[click] 
An easy test, if your data scientists can get it in 10 minutes then it might be a good choice.

## {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
*Day one decides whether people keep going.*
:::

::: {.notes}
Not all APIs are created equal — some are thin wrappers exposing every
private method. A user-friendly framework pays off while people are
still coming up to speed on everything else.

The goal is comfort, not full control of a complex system.
:::

## Easiest means: the same shape of thought {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- Easy [syntax]{.accent} is a virtue
- Import your [philosophy]{.accent}
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM)
"So that's day one. The second thing easiest means is
about every day after: the Data Scientist doesn't have to relearn how to
think about data."

TODO: Point 1 and 2 are too similar, even the code snippets are too alike.

[click]
Easy syntax — other options leaned on verbose, heavily-typed
languages that added friction before anyone got to the actual work.

[click]
Import your philosophy — Polars' expression API preserves the
dplyr way of thinking about data, not just its syntax. select,
transform, filter, aggregate — no detour through OOP, strong typing, or
imperative loops.
:::

## Same thought, different language

`sum(revenue[status == "paid"])` becomes:

```python
pl.col("revenue")
  .filter(pl.col("status") == "paid")
  .sum()
```

::: {.fragment}
**Easiest = the same sentence, in a new language.**
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM)
This is a knowledge transfer instead of a migration.
Once you know the syntax, does the system let you keep thinking about data the way you already do?


Subset a vector by a condition, then reduce it. Same thought. The R
version is a bracket; the Polars version is a chain — but it's the same
sentence.

[click] Nobody wrote a for loop. The vectorized mental model came with
us. That's the property to look for: the option where your old
sentences still parse.

TODO: The 3rd snippet is identical to the first point. All the snippets are too similar!

:::

## Same thought, every column {.code-stack}

::: {.fragment}
**dplyr**

```r
df |>
  mutate(across(
    starts_with("rev"),
    \(x) x * 1.1
  ))
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Polars**

```python
import polars.selectors as cs

df.with_columns(
  cs.starts_with("rev") * 1.1
)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .center}
**Easiest = you didn't learn a new way to think.**
:::

::: {.notes}
[click] dplyr — pick columns by a rule, apply one expression to all.

[click] Polars — same idea. `cs` is Polars' column selectors.

TODO: I like the explanation but again, too similar.

[click] Same idea, both sides. The chain is the pipe; the expression is
the thing inside `across`. Again — the point isn't that Polars has
selectors; it's that the easy option is the one where the Data Scientist
didn't have to learn a new way to think.

Morale beat lives here: when everyone writes it this way, code is
readable and reviewable across the team. Shared idioms mean the whole
team has the *same* migration, not eight different ones.
:::

## {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
Some days, you don't need to learn anything new.
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM)
Migration is already information overload.
It doesn't all have to land on day one. You don't take Calc 4 before Calc 1.

Once people are comfortable, they move on to the fancier stuff on their
own, and make better-informed decisions about it.

Riff:
- whether that's typing, understanding types in the first place
- Classes to represent behavior
- Getting fancy with magic methods in python, or the finer things a language has to offer

(VERBATIM)
I remember personally moving some code to rust for performance and after I got comfertable
I got used to macros and traits, which would've been complete overkill to start.

:::

# Ask the Data Scientist

## Next time you're in that room {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- Ask: *does it work on [day one]{.accent}?*
- Ask: *does my old [sentence]{.accent} still parse?*
- Ask: *who [asked]{.accent} the Data Scientist?*
:::

::: {.notes}
(VERBATIM)
So here's what I'd like you to take out of this room.

(VERBATIM)
You will be in a migration meeting. Finance, leadership, tech, and
cyber will all have an opinion. Three questions to bring:

[click] 
(VERBATIM)
Day one — can someone write real, useful code before they've mastered environments and types?

[click] 
(VERBATIM)
Old sentence — take a line you write every week in the old language. 
Does it translate, or does it need a detour?

[click] 
(VERBATIM)
Who asked the Data Scientist — if the answer is "no one," you're the one who has to.

:::
